rules.message: Hardcoded secret-shaped literal (a SECRET_KEY/API-key/password/token assignment, or a known cloud-key prefix). `secret_key` is spelled as its own alternative rather than adding a bare `key` to the name list, and that is a measured choice, not a stylistic one: Django/Flask/Rails all commit their signing key as `SECRET_KEY = "..."`, and the name arms match a keyword that the identifier ENDS with, so `secret` alone never reached it — a committed Django SECRET_KEY was invisible to both secret rules until 2026-08-18. Adding bare `key` also catches it, and over a 17-repo corpus it brought 46 more findings of which one was a credential: the rest were `DECIDER_KEY = "enable_very_recent_tweets"`, `HEADER_KEY = "Authorization"`, `key: 'username'`. `secret[_-]?key` catches the same real leak and added exactly the one finding. If you are about to widen this list from a config vocabulary, measure that trade first: `vocabulary.secretParamNames` is a URL-PARAMETER vocabulary, where `key` is unambiguous because the context is a query string, and it does not mean the same thing as an identifier name in a source literal. A credential committed to source is exposed to every reader/fork/clone and cannot be rotated without a code change. BEFORE ROTATING, FIND WHAT IS STILL USING THIS VALUE — deploys, CI jobs, cron, inbound webhooks, sibling services, and any third-party console it was pasted into. Rotation is not additive: issuing the replacement invalidates the old value at that instant, so every holder you did not migrate starts failing auth (401) as you finish, and that outage is noticed before the leak is. Where the issuer will hold two live values, use an OVERLAPPING WINDOW — mint the new one, move each consumer, revoke the old; where it holds only one, swap in a coordinated window with those owners on hand. Urgency and coordination are not in tension: a leaked value is compromised NOW, and a cutover is arranged in minutes, not releases. IF this value is a real credential: move it to an environment variable or a secrets manager (e.g. `process.env.API_KEY`, or `std::env::var` in Rust) — but that only stops the NEXT leak, because the value is already exposed via git history and any forks/clones that pulled it, so rotate/revoke the actual credential too. The conditional is load-bearing rather than hedging, and this rule scans test paths too, not just application code: a committed literal IS committed wherever it sits, so a real staging credential inside a fixture is a real leak — but so is `password="password"`, and rotating that is not a thing anyone can do. Measured over a 17-repo corpus (2026-08-18) this rule fired 55 times and the majority of hits were test fixtures of exactly that shape. Judge the VALUE first; if there is no credential to revoke, the finding is telling you a literal exists, not that you have been breached. The match is NOT on the property name alone — a VALUE-SHAPE gate rejects identifier-shaped values: any literal built from letter-only words joined by `-`/`_`/`.` (`"mantine-DatePickerInput-input"`, `"refresh-token"`, `"MY_API_KEY"`, `"jwt.token.here"`) is a CSS class / selector / constant name / placeholder, not a credential, and is dropped in any casing. What the gate does NOT reject is punctuation: the value is any non-space, non-quote run of 8+ characters, so `"Pr0d!Postgres#2024"` is seen. WHY THE FLOOR IS 8 AND NOT 9, since that one character decides more of this rule's output than anything else in it: 8 is the minimum length nearly every password policy mandates, so it is the shortest run that can be a real password, and the floor is DERIVED from the class being hunted rather than picked for roundness. It is also load-bearing rather than a formality, which was measured on 2026-08-29 over nine trees (calcom/cal.com, dotnet/eShop, three small front ends, immich, koel, macrozheng/mall, nocodb) with three clean release builds one character apart: this rule reports 152 findings at 8, 86 at 9, and 170 at 7 — so raising the floor by one would drop 66 of the 152 (43%) and lowering it by one adds 18. Nearly half this rule's output sits exactly ON the boundary, and most of those 8-character values are weak fixture literals rather than live credentials. That is an argument for judging the VALUE, which the paragraph above already asks you to do, and NOT for a longer floor: an 8-character credential that is real is precisely the weak credential worth reporting, and a floor of 9 silences every one of them to buy quiet. It did not use to be — until 2026-08-16 the value had to be drawn from `[A-Za-z0-9+/_-]`, which meant one `!` or `#` turned the rule off, and the sensitivity therefore ran BACKWARDS against the characters every password policy mandates (`"hunter2hunter2xx"` reported, `"hunter2hunter2!x"` silent). High-entropy string literal bound to a secret-named binding (name ending in secret-key/api-key/apikey/secret/passwd/password/token). `secret_key` is spelled as its own alternative rather than adding a bare `key` to the name list, and that is a measured choice, not a stylistic one: Django/Flask/Rails all commit their signing key as `SECRET_KEY = "..."`, and the name arms match a keyword that the identifier ENDS with, so `secret` alone never reached it — a committed Django SECRET_KEY was invisible to both secret rules until 2026-08-18. This rule reads the string-literal-with-binding-name IR node (name + value hash + value entropy, NEVER the value itself — nothing secret-shaped is written to the analysis cache), which is exactly the fix `hardcoded-secret`'s message used to name as its own ceiling: that line scan's identifier-shape veto killed a dictionary-word passphrase (`"correct-horse-battery-staple"`, 97.9 total Shannon bits) identically to a CSS class name, and killed a random base64url token whenever it drew no digits. The judgment here is MEASURED ENTROPY, not value shape: total Shannon bits over the value's bytes, threshold 80 (measured separation, 2026-08-03: 4-word passphrases p5 = 83.0 so 2.9% are missed; 24-char no-digit base64url tokens floor = 85.0 so 0% missed; the hardest true negatives sit below — `"PlaceholderSecretValue"` 75.7, `"a7Fk29QmZx41Lp08Wd"` 75.1, `"refresh_token"` 41.4). Three vetoes, each stated with what it cannot do: a value LITERALLY equal to its own binding name is dropped by hash equality (`refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — exact equality only, a hash cannot case-fold); a mock/test/fake/dummy/sample/placeholder/example word in the binding NAME is dropped, boundary-anchored (name start, `-`/`_`, digit, or a camelCase transition — `mockApiKey`/`test_secret`/`myTestToken` are vetoed; `latestToken`/`attestationSecret`, which merely EMBED `test`, keep firing); but a placeholder word in the VALUE is invisible by design — a value-side veto is structurally impossible here because the channel never carries the value (it is reduced to hash + entropy at extraction, the same choice that keeps candidate secrets out of the plain-text cache) — so a long placeholder or i18n value bound to a clean secret name relies on sitting under the 80-bit floor, and one that clears it fires. Remaining blindness, measured rather than guessed: a WEAK sub-floor credential (`password`, `admin123456`) never reaches this rule — a short or low-diversity string sits under any useful floor by construction, and that class is the sibling `hardcoded-secret` line scan's to catch; an English-word identifier chain long enough to clear the floor (`"mantine-DatePickerInput-input"`, 107.4 bits) is indistinguishable from a passphrase by any content-free statistic, so when bound to a secret-ending name it fires — that direction (noise on secret-named bindings) is chosen over the old silence; and 3-word passphrases mostly sit under the floor (88.5% below 80) — a floor low enough to catch them would swallow the placeholder negatives above. Digit-carrying values and known vendor prefixes are `hardcoded-secret`'s (unchanged) line-scan business, so one committed `sk_live_…` can legitimately carry both findings. A credential committed to source is exposed to every reader/fork/clone and cannot be rotated without a code change. BEFORE ROTATING, FIND WHAT IS STILL USING THIS VALUE — deploys, CI jobs, cron, inbound webhooks, sibling services, and any third-party console it was pasted into. Rotation is not additive: issuing the replacement invalidates the old value at that instant, so every holder you did not migrate starts failing auth (401) as you finish, and that outage is noticed before the leak is. Where the issuer will hold two live values, use an OVERLAPPING WINDOW — mint the new one, move each consumer, revoke the old; where it holds only one, swap in a coordinated window with those owners on hand. Urgency and coordination are not in tension: a leaked value is compromised NOW, and a cutover is arranged in minutes, not releases. Rotate/revoke the actual credential, then move the replacement to an environment variable or a secrets manager. This rule fires only in languages whose parser projects the channel (TS/JS, Python, Java, C#, Go, Rust — silence elsewhere is no-evidence, never clean), which is an EXTENSION set and not merely a language set: a `.vue`/`.svelte` single-file component carries TypeScript inside a `<script>` block, `dispatch_by_extension` routes those extensions to no parser, and so a secret bound in an SFC never reaches this channel — while the sibling line scan `security/hardcoded-secret` DOES read that text and does report it, so the two rules disagree about the same literal by design. That SFC disagreement is now the only place the two rules diverge IN FILE REACH -- which is a claim about which files each one opens and nothing more. On the files they BOTH read they still disagree constantly, and that is the design: this rule needs a measured 80-bit floor and a parser-projected binding, the line scan needs a shape and a name, so `apiKey = "correcthorsebattery"` is a line-scan finding and silent here, while a high-entropy value under a name the line scan's list does not carry is the reverse. The reach claim was not true until 2026-08-21: this pattern stopped at `ts|tsx|js|mjs|cjs` on the JS side while the line scan gained `jsx|mts|cts` on 2026-08-20, so a React tree's `.jsx` secret reported `security/hardcoded-secret` and nothing from this rule — measured with the same literal in `src/config.jsx` and `src/config.ts`, which produced one finding and two. The TypeScript frontend claims all three extensions (`dispatch_by_extension` maps `jsx` to TypeScript and the parser enables JSX syntax for it), so that was reach this build already had and this rule was not asking for. The SFC gap is the one that remains, and it is a parser question rather than a pattern one. This rule also scans test regions (a committed fixture credential still has to be rotated). Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-high-entropy-secret-ok` (`#` comments work too).

A high-entropy secret value is committed in a configuration file (`jwt.secret`, `*.password`, `api-key`, ... in a config file — `.properties`, `.ya?ml`, `.toml`, `.ini`, `.conf`, `.cfg`, `.json`/`.jsonc`, or `.env`) — this is a live credential exposed to every reader/fork/clone AND preserved in git history, and unlike a code literal it is often the app's real signing key or datastore password. Move it to an environment variable or secrets manager referenced from config (`jwt.secret=${JWT_SECRET}`). BEFORE ROTATING, FIND WHAT IS STILL USING THIS VALUE — deploys, CI jobs, cron, inbound webhooks, sibling services, and any third-party console it was pasted into. Rotation is not additive: issuing the replacement invalidates the old value at that instant, so every holder you did not migrate starts failing auth (401) as you finish, and that outage is noticed before the leak is. Where the issuer will hold two live values, use an OVERLAPPING WINDOW — mint the new one, move each consumer, revoke the old; where it holds only one, swap in a coordinated window with those owners on hand. Urgency and coordination are not in tension: a leaked value is compromised NOW, and a cutover is arranged in minutes, not releases. Then rotate/revoke the committed value. FIVE THINGS ARE NOT FLAGGED, and the last of them is a WORD VOCABULARY rather than a shape: an empty value; a value under 16 characters; a `${VAR}`/`$VAR` env reference; an `<angle-bracket>` fill-in, or a LINE (not a value - this arm alone was never re-scoped to value position) carrying `changeme`/`change_me`/`change-me`/`your_`/`your-`/`placeholder`/`example`/`redacted`/`xxxx` anywhere on it; and - added 2026-08-20 and NOT stated here until 2026-08-20, which is the reason this sentence is now the long one - a value that STARTS with `mock`/`test`/`fake`/`dummy`/`sample`/`placeholder`/`example`/`your`/`changeme`/`redacted` followed by a separator, a digit, an uppercase letter, or the end of the value. That last arm is anchored to VALUE POSITION (it must sit after the `=`/`:`), which is what keeps a real secret alive next to a comment that happens to say "example" - but it is a judgment about a WORD, not about entropy or shape, and it is wrong in exactly one direction: a placeholder-sounding prefix on a real credential. Measured shapes it kills: `password: testDatabaseSecretPassword` and `token: sampleButRealProductionToken1` each report NOTHING. What that buys is concrete rather than theoretical - a Spring `application-test.yml` whose staging database password really is spelled `testPassword...` is silent here, and the two sibling rules that DO read config files judge something else entirely - `security/private-key-committed` wants a PEM block and `security/vendor-token-committed` wants a known vendor prefix, and a database password is neither - so nothing in this pack recovers it. It was taken because admitting `.json` made dotnet/eShop's five `Password=yourWeak(!)Password` lines reachable in one step and none of them is a credential; the trade is five known false positives against this class of silence, and it belongs in the finding rather than only in the tests, because the tests do not ship with the finding. THE VALUE NO LONGER HAS TO END THE LINE, and the anchor that required it was a silence, not a narrowing. Until 2026-08-20 the pattern ended `["']?\s*$`, so a single trailing comment turned the rule off for the whole file type it was written for. Measured on macrozheng/mall, which writes EVERY committed secret with a trailing comment: `secret: mall-admin-secret #<comment>` reported nothing while the byte-identical `secret: mall-admin-secret` alone on its line reported a finding, and a scan of that tree returned ZERO config secrets while it carried two JWT signing keys. The tail now admits a `#`/`;`/`//` comment and one JSON structural closer (`,`/`}`/`]`) — the closer is what makes `.json` reachable at all, since a JSON value never ends its own line. THE VALUE ALPHABET IS NO LONGER RESTRICTED. It was `[A-Za-z0-9+/_-]`, which meant one `!` or `#` in the value turned the rule off — the sensitivity ran BACKWARDS against the characters every password policy mandates. It is now any run of non-space, non-quote characters, so `Password=Pr0d!Pg#2024` is seen. The sibling `security/hardcoded-secret` made the identical correction on 2026-08-16 for source literals; this rule kept the old alphabet for four days longer. WHAT IT STILL CANNOT SEE, stated because this rule's silence is easy to read as clean: the value must be 16+ characters, so the weak credentials that dominate real committed configs are OUT OF REACH BY CONSTRUCTION — `password: 123456`, `password: root` and `accessKey: minioadmin` are each under the floor and each report nothing, including when they sit in a production Spring profile. The floor is KEPT rather than lowered, and the trade is measured (2026-08-20) rather than asserted: dropping it to 6 characters across macrozheng/mall, dotnet/eShop and koel/koel adds 14 lines, of which 8 are real committed credentials (mall's prod-profile MySQL password in three services, its MinIO access/secret key pair in two profiles, and a MinIO root password in a compose file) and 6 are ephemeral CI-service passwords under `.github/workflows/` (`MYSQL_PASSWORD: mariadb`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres`, `PASSWORD: Pass123$`). A length floor carries no shape or entropy judgment and cannot separate those; entropy can, and that is `security/high-entropy-secret`'s channel — which reads a PARSER-projected literal channel and therefore never reads a config file at all. Until one of the two grows the other's half, a weak literal password in configuration is nobody's finding. ONE WHOLE FILE CLASS IS SKIPPED BEFORE ANY LINE IS READ, and it is a PATH judgment rather than a value one: TRANSLATION CATALOGUES. A file under a `locales/`, `locale/` or `i18n/` directory whose NEXT path component is a BCP-47 language tag is not scanned - the tag either being a directory (`packages/i18n/locales/km/common.json`, `public/locales/ja-JP/grafana.json`) or the file's own stem (`i18n/nb_NO.json`, `i18n/fil.json`). BOTH HALVES ARE REQUIRED, which is what keeps `packages/i18n/locales/config.json` and `packages/i18n/package.json` judged, and what keeps a language-shaped directory OUTSIDE such a container untouched - `no` is Norwegian and also an ordinary directory name, so `deploy/no/application.yml` still reports. WHY: the 16-character value floor is a proxy for "looks like a secret" and it collapses in writing systems that do not separate words with spaces, so this rule read translated UI labels as credentials and did so UNEVENLY. Measured on calcom/cal.com `176037d`: 50 of its 59 findings were locale strings, distributed km 24 / ja 14 / zh 5 / de 2 / fi 2 / da, no, sv 1 each - German compounds landing beside the non-Latin scripts for the same reason. immich `i18n/<tag>.json` contributed 17 more and grafana `public/locales/<tag>/*.json` 20; all 87 were read one at a time and not one was a credential. WHAT THIS DOES NOT COVER, measured and declined rather than overlooked, because widening to a direction that suppresses nothing buys only risk: `lang/<tag>.json` (nocodb, 40 files, 0 findings), `translations/<tag>/*.json` (grafana, 19 files, 0 findings) and the Java ResourceBundle `messages/messages_<tag>.properties` (spring-petclinic, 9 files, 0 findings) are all still scanned. THE COST, stated because a suppressed finding leaves no trace: a credential committed INSIDE a translation catalogue is now out of this rule's reach entirely, and no `exclude`-style config key can put it back - the lever is the pack (`packs: { extraDirs: [...] }`). `security/private-key-committed` and `security/vendor-token-committed` do still read those files, and a PEM block or a vendor-prefixed token there is still reported. Suppress a vetted case with `# zzop-config-file-secret-ok` in the `.properties`, `.yaml`/`.yml`, `.toml`, `.ini`, `.conf`, `.cfg` and `.env` files this rule reads. A strict `.json` has no comment syntax at all, so nothing can be written on the line and the only lever there is config (`rules: {"security/config-file-secret": "off"}`, or an `exclude` path). A `.jsonc` takes `// zzop-config-file-secret-ok`.

A secret-shaped query parameter (`api_key`/`access_token`/`token`/`secret`) appears in a URL — URLs are logged by proxies, load balancers, browser history and the `Referer` header. Move the credential into an `Authorization` header (or body/cookie) instead. In a `.py` file the suppression marker is spelled `# zzop-api-key-in-url-ok` instead.

A server-only-shaped env var (`SECRET`/`PRIVATE`/`SERVICE_ROLE`/`SERVICE_KEY`) is referenced from frontend code — build tools inline `process.env.*`/`import.meta.env.*` into the shipped JS bundle, making it readable in devtools. PATH SCOPE, disclosed because a security rule's silence reads as a clean bill of health when it is not one: "frontend code" here means exactly two things — ANY `.tsx`/`.jsx`/`.vue`/`.svelte` file anywhere in the tree (single-file components joined on 2026-08-20: an SFC is front-end source by definition, and its `<script setup>` block is the plainest place a bundled secret can sit), or any other JS/TS-family file (`.ts`/`.mts`/`.cts`/`.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`) under a path segment literally named `fe`, `frontend`, `client` or `web`. THREE SERVER-ONLY PATH SHAPES ARE CARVED BACK OUT of that scope, and what justifies each is that the FRAMEWORK fixes its spelling rather than the project choosing it: a Next.js App Router ROUTE HANDLER (a file named `route.ts`/`.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`/`.mts`/`.cts` under an `app/` segment), a Pages Router API route (anything under `pages/api/` with one of those same non-component extensions), and `next.config.*`. None of the three can reach a client bundle, and without the carve-out this rule reports every server file of a monorepo that names its application directory `web` — which is the default Next.js/Turborepo layout, so the cost is not a corner case (measured on one such repository: six findings, five of them these shapes and none of them reachable from a browser). The carve-out is deliberately the SHAPE OF THAT CONVENTION and not the broader property it happens to have. It is not "a path containing `api`": a directory someone named `api` that holds real client code is still scanned, an App Router route handler OUTSIDE any `api/` segment is still exempt (Next does not require that segment — the FILENAME is its declaration), and the `pages/api/` arm declines `.vue`/`.svelte` so a Nuxt or SvelteKit tree, where `pages/` holds PAGES, cannot be swept in by the directory name alone. Everything else under the same app directory keeps being scanned, including a helper module sitting beside a route handler, a `page.tsx`/`layout.tsx` under `app/`, and a plain script at the application root — a server-only Node script whose path carries no framework declaration still reports here, because inferring server-ness from anything weaker than a declaration is how a security rule goes quiet on real leaks. A plain `.ts`/`.js` module that is nonetheless bundled into the client (`src/lib/api.ts` in a Next.js app, a `shared/`/`common/` helper, a non-`.tsx` file under `app/`/`pages/`/`components/`) is never scanned, and `.mjs`/`.cjs` outside one of those four path segments are not scanned at all. A `process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` in `src/lib/api.ts` is therefore invisible here: zero findings from this rule means "not scanned there", never "no server-only secret reaches the bundle". If the value is genuinely secret, the only correct fix is moving its use behind a backend endpoint (proxy it server-side) — do not just rename it with a `NEXT_PUBLIC_`/`VITE_` prefix. AND THE PREFIX DOES NOT SILENCE THIS FINDING — said here because a prescription you can follow exactly and still see red is worse than no prescription at all. Only reach for that prefix if the value was never actually secret to begin with (e.g. a public config flag flagged by mistake). The name test reads `SECRET`/`PRIVATE`/`SERVICE_ROLE`/`SERVICE_KEY` ANYWHERE in the variable name, so `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` matches exactly as `process.env.SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` does (measured, both report). That is deliberate rather than an oversight: prefixing a service-role key with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` is the one rename that makes the leak certain instead of likely, and a rule that went quiet for it would be endorsing it. So when the value really was never secret, the green path is not the rename — it is `// zzop-secret-env-in-fe-ok` on the finding's line or the line directly above it, or turning the rule off for that path in config (`rules: {"security/secret-env-in-fe": "off"}`, or an `exclude` entry). In a `.vue`/`.svelte` `<template>` block, wrap that marker in an HTML comment so it does not render on the page — `<!-- // zzop-secret-env-in-fe-ok -->`. The `//` is what the marker table reads and dropping it (`<!-- zzop-secret-env-in-fe-ok -->`) suppresses nothing; inside a `<script>` block the plain `//` form is ordinary.

BEFORE ROTATING, FIND WHAT IS STILL USING THIS VALUE — deploys, CI jobs, cron, inbound webhooks, sibling services, and any third-party console it was pasted into. Rotation is not additive: issuing the replacement invalidates the old value at that instant, so every holder you did not migrate starts failing auth (401) as you finish, and that outage is noticed before the leak is. Read it from an environment variable, an excluded properties file, or a secrets manager — but that only stops the NEXT leak: this password is already exposed via git history and any forks/clones that pulled it, so rotate/revoke the actual credential too.

A connection-string URL embeds a password directly in source (`scheme://user:pass@host`) — anyone with repo read access effectively owns the datastore, and git history preserves the credential even after it's later removed from HEAD. Move the URL to environment/secret configuration. An INTERPOLATED userinfo slot is not flagged, in every language this rule scans: a `${...}` template placeholder, a `{{...}}`/`<...>` template hole, a `process.env` read, or a Rust `format!`/`write!` placeholder (`{}`, `{name}`, `{0}`) sitting between `://` and `@` means the password is not in this source line at all — there is nothing here to rotate, and saying otherwise would send a reader chasing a credential that does not exist. That veto stays anchored to the userinfo slot: a placeholder in the HOST slot does not launder a password spelled literally before the `@`. A printf-family format verb in the PASSWORD slot (`%s`/`%v`/`%q` — Go's `fmt.Sprintf`, Python's `%`-format, C's `printf`) is vetoed too, on a WEAKER claim that is stated rather than blurred into the four above: printf ARGUMENTS sit on the same line by construction, so `fmt.Sprintf("postgres://%s:%s@%s/db", user, "S3cr3tPw9!", host)` is not reported even though its credential is still on screen, and no sibling rule picks that up. Across the corpus this costs nothing — the one instance with a literal in the arguments spells it `"password"`, which the placeholder arm vetoes anyway — but it is a gap rather than an absence. The printf arm is anchored one slot tighter than the others — to the password itself — because `http://%s:testpass@%s` formats the USERNAME and then spells the password out; and it reads a verb as `%` followed by a letter that is NOT a hex digit, which is exactly what tells a format verb from a percent-ENCODED character (`%HH` is always `%` plus two hex digits). That shape was measured 2026-08-24 over 57 of the 58 checkouts before it was written: it drops 49 findings that are every one of them a `%s` placeholder (48 in grafana's integration tests, plus one SQLAlchemy `%`-format), where a looser `%` shape would also have erased the 15 surviving findings whose password slot carries a `%` at all, every one of them a REAL percent-ENCODED password — `pass%20pass`, `apples%2Foranges`, `%70ass` — which are exactly the findings this rule exists for. Loopback hosts (localhost/127.0.0.1) and placeholder passwords are not flagged, and the second of those is judged by SHAPE rather than a name alone: a password slot that is nothing but a short run of letters (`tiger`, `p`, `bar`, `pass`) carries no entropy and is not a credential anyone could use, alongside the named spellings (`changeme`, `passwd`, `mypwd`, ...) that are longer than the shape admits. The shape arm was added 2026-08-19 after measuring 19 upstream checkouts: this rule produced 69 findings and ALL 69 were documentation examples, 36 of them `scott:tiger` — Oracle's demo account, which SQLAlchemy writes into every dialect docstring — and 17 `u:p`. Only `user:pass` was on the name list, which is the failure mode a hand-written veto always has: everything the author did not think of stays reported forever. The trade is stated rather than hidden: a REAL password that is also a short bare word is now missed, which is the same bargain the sibling `hardcoded-secret` strikes with identifier-shaped values, and the boundary is drawn where placeholders stop — seven letters still fires, and so does any password carrying a digit or punctuation (`tiger^5HHH` is reported). suppress a remaining vetted sample with `// zzop-conn-string-credentials-ok`. In a `.py` file the suppression marker is spelled `# zzop-conn-string-credentials-ok` instead.

`$queryRawUnsafe`/`$executeRawUnsafe` called — these run the given SQL as-is with no parameterization, so any request-derived string interpolated into it is a SQL injection. THE TAGGED TEMPLATE PARAMETERIZES EVERY `${...}`, WHICH IS THE SAME REASON THE UNSAFE CALL EXISTS: a bound parameter can stand only where the database expects a VALUE, so an interpolation that supplies an IDENTIFIER — a table name, the column in an `ORDER BY`, a schema picked per tenant — does not survive the rewrite. A table name interpolated into the tagged form reaches the server as `SELECT * FROM $1` and comes back a syntax error; an `ORDER BY` column is the worse half because it is ACCEPTED — a parameter in that position is read as a constant, so the rows arrive in whatever order the plan happened to produce and nothing raises. Sort the interpolations before you rewrite: values go straight into the tagged template, and each identifier needs a fixed map from the request's string to a literal you wrote, or `Prisma.raw` around that fragment alone — which re-opens this finding for whatever you hand it, so it has to receive a value you chose and never one the request supplied. Use `$queryRaw`/`$executeRaw` tagged templates (or pass values as separate arguments) so Prisma parameterizes the query.

JPA `@Query` built via string concatenation (`@Query("..." + ...)`). So there is no injection path to analyze in this position, by language rule rather than by the limits of this matcher — do not re-escalate this rule on the theory that better annotation parsing would find one. What remains is hygiene: a concatenated `@Query` hides the full statement from review and makes future refactors error-prone. Prefer a single literal, with named parameters (`:param` with `@Param`) for values. The RUNTIME sibling `security/sql-string-concat` is the injectable shape — string concatenation in ordinary code, where nothing constrains the operand to a constant — and it keeps its higher severity for exactly that reason.

A SQL string is built by concatenating an expression into the statement text — if the concatenated part is request-derived, this is SQL injection (the input rewrites the query); even a constant fragment hides that risk from review. A PLACEHOLDER CAN STAND ONLY WHERE THE DATABASE EXPECTS A VALUE, SO NOT EVERY INTERPOLATION HAS A BOUND FORM TO MOVE TO: a table name, a schema chosen per tenant, and the column or direction in an `ORDER BY` are IDENTIFIERS, and no driver parameterizes an identifier — an `IN (...)` list needs one placeholder per element rather than one for the list. The two failures are not equally kind. A table name put in a placeholder reaches the server as `SELECT * FROM ?` and comes back a syntax error you cannot miss; an `ORDER BY` column there is ACCEPTED as a constant, so the rows arrive in whatever order the plan happened to produce and nothing is raised. Sort the interpolations before you rewrite: values become placeholders plus bound arguments, and each identifier needs a fixed map from the request string to a literal you wrote — never the request string itself, escaped or quoted. Use a parameterized/bound query instead (PreparedStatement `?`, JPA `:named` + setParameter) — never escape values into the string. Annotation lines are excluded — element values are compile-time constants (JLS 9.7.1), so the request-derived claim above is structurally false there, and `annotation-sql-concat` owns that shape at info.

A tainted-source access (request body/query/params/headers, `searchParams`, `process.argv`) and a dangerous sink (`eval`, `new Function`, `exec`/`spawn`, raw SQL, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `.innerHTML`) both appear in the same function — this is a coarse v1 check (source+sink co-occurrence, not real dataflow), so confirm the value is actually tainted here. Kept at `warning`, not `critical`: co-occurrence is an approximation of dataflow, not proof of it, and `critical` is reserved for matchers that can prove their claim — treat a hit as a lead to confirm, not a confirmed exploit. For a SQL sink, parameterize the query (prepared/parameterized statement API) — never escape or interpolate the tainted value into the SQL string. For a shell/process-exec sink, use `execFile`/`spawn` with an args array, not a shell-string `exec()` with string concatenation. For a DOM/HTML sink, use `textContent` (not `innerHTML`) for plain text, or a vetted HTML-sanitizer library if HTML must be inserted — never raw `innerHTML` with tainted input.

`eval(...)` called with a non-literal argument, or `new Function(...)` used at all (even with only literal arguments — constructing a function from a string at runtime still defeats CSP's `script-src` and is invisible to every static analyzer downstream, so it is a code smell worth surfacing regardless) — building and executing code from a runtime string is one of the highest-risk sinks in JS: if any part of that string can be influenced by user input, it's arbitrary code execution. EACH SUBSTITUTE IS NARROWER THAN WHAT IT REPLACES, AND THE INPUTS THAT NO LONGER FIT FAIL AT RUNTIME ON REAL DATA RATHER THAN IN REVIEW: JSON is a strict subset of the object syntax `eval` accepted, so a payload carrying unquoted keys, single-quoted strings, a trailing comma, a comment, `undefined`, `NaN` or a `new Date(...)` parsed yesterday and throws a `SyntaxError` out of `JSON.parse` today — and the legacy shape this rule most often flags, an `eval` wrapping a parenthesised object literal, is exactly a producer of that dialect. A lookup table replaces a fixed set of NAMES, not an expression language: where the string being built is arithmetic, a filter predicate or a template someone authored, there is no table to write and the honest answer is a real parser for the small language you actually accept. Read a sample of the strings this call has received in production before you pick one — the substitute is decided by that dialect, not by the call site. Avoid dynamic code construction; use a plain function/lookup table/JSON.parse instead. Note: `security/taint-flow` already covers `eval` when a request-derived source co-occurs in the same function, `.ts`/`.tsx` only; this rule is source-free (fires on the construct itself, not just a proven-tainted case) and also covers `.js`/`.jsx`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`. When they are connected, and the concatenated part is request-derived, it is command injection. One Rust function PROVEN by the parser's projected call-site channel to construct an OS process (a `Command::new(...)` call, in its `std::process::`-qualified, `process::`-qualified or bare spelling — each kept as written) ALSO builds a string with a `format!`/`write!`/`writeln!` macro (that half stays LEXICAL and is where this finding anchors; the structural witness retires the string/comment false-fire class of the old regex, at a disclosed cost: a construction this engine cannot parse, or one reached through an aliased path, projects no site and the rule is silent there — absence of evidence, never a clean bill) — if that string reaches the PROGRAM NAME (`Command::new(formatted)`) or is routed through a shell (`Command::new("sh").arg("-c").arg(formatted)`) with a request-derived value, that is command injection. Read the command string before you rewrite it — with no shell metacharacter in it the split is mechanical, and with one the pipeline has to move into the calling program: wire the pipe through the child stdio, write the child output yourself instead of redirecting, expand the glob with a directory read. Turning the shell back on to make the argv form work again restores the exact injection this finding is about. Pass every argument as its own `.arg(value)` rather than building one shell string, do not route through `sh -c`, and validate or allow-list any caller-supplied part.
