That gate is also why this rule's `file_pattern` stops at the extensions a parser claims while its `line-scan` siblings in this pack gained `.vue`/`.svelte` on 2026-08-20: an SFC dispatches to no language, so it projects no call site and this rule could never fire in one. Listing the extension would have advertised coverage the substrate cannot deliver, and `crates/engine`'s capability matrix says so in the same words (it failed the widening on exactly this rule and no other). Boundary: `security/taint-flow` also flags `exec`/`execSync` as a sink, but only when a request-derived source co-occurs in the same `.ts`/`.tsx` function; this rule needs no source, fires on the interpolation shape alone, and also covers plain `.js` files — treat the two as complementary, not redundant. Cross-language siblings under the same concept name, deliberately weaker: Java `security/cmd-injection` and Rust `security/command-and-interpolation` are both `warning`, because the APIs they match (`Runtime.exec`'s whitespace tokenization, `Command::new`'s direct argv spawn) hand nothing to a shell — this rule alone is `critical` because `exec`/`execSync`'s command string IS handed to a shell, so a dynamic segment needs no further conditions to become injection.

One Python or Go function PROVEN by the parser's projected call-site channel to construct an OS process ALSO builds a string by concatenation or interpolation (that half stays LEXICAL and is where this finding anchors). The recognized constructors are exactly the platform APIs each producer pins — Python's `subprocess.run` / `subprocess.call` / `subprocess.check_call` / `subprocess.check_output` / `subprocess.Popen` / `os.system` / `os.popen`, and Go's `exec.Command` / `exec.CommandContext` — each matched by its written spelling, so a bare-name import (`from subprocess import run` → `run(...)`) or a third-party runner (`sh`, `plumbum`) projects no site and this rule is silent there: absence of evidence, never a clean bill. `ALSO` is literal: this is CO-OCCURRENCE within one function body, not proof that the built string is the one that gets executed (the two may be unrelated statements), which is why it is `warning` and not `critical` — the same standing the Java sibling `security/cmd-injection` and the Rust sibling `security/command-and-interpolation` take. Whether a real hit is command injection or merely argument injection depends on which spelling reached the process, and the two languages differ: Python's `os.system` and `os.popen` hand the whole string to a SHELL, as does `subprocess.*` called with `shell=True`, so a request-derived part there injects shell syntax (`;`, `|`, backticks) and is command injection outright; `subprocess.*` with an argv LIST and Go's `exec.Command` spawn the program directly with no shell, so the worst an argument-position value enables is argument/option injection against the called program — real exposure, but not command injection. Go's shell-routed spelling is the explicit `exec.Command("sh", "-c", built)`, and that one carries the full injection risk. This rule does not distinguish those cases, because the co-occurrence gate above means it has not established WHICH string reached the process — reading the argv shape would be a claim about a link this matcher never proved. The interpolation half is pinned to one quote character at a time, for the reason its SQL sibling `security/sql-interpolated-statement` states at length: a body class excluding both quotes stops at a literal's own inner quote and misreads the rest of the line. WHERE A SHELL WAS DOING THE WORK, THE ARGV FORM DOES NOT DO IT, AND WHAT BREAKS FAILS QUIETLY: a `|` pipe, a `>` redirect, `&&`/`;` sequencing, a `*` glob, `$VAR` expansion and a `~` home reference are parsed by the shell, so the moment those parts become inert argv elements the command stops meaning what it meant — it does not raise, it runs the first program against the rest as literal filenames. The whitespace split goes with it: one interpolated value that used to expand into several tokens now arrives as ONE argument, and the called program rejects it or reads it as a filename. Read the command string before you rewrite it — with no shell metacharacter in it the split is mechanical, and with one the pipeline has to move into the calling program: wire the pipe through the child stdio, write the child output yourself instead of redirecting, expand the glob with a directory read. Turning the shell back on to make the argv form work again restores the exact injection this finding is about. Pass every argument as its own list element or `exec.Command` argument rather than building one shell string, leave `shell=True` off and never route through `sh -c`, and validate or allow-list any caller-supplied part. In a `.py` file the suppression marker is spelled `# zzop-command-interpolated-string-ok` instead.

`DocumentBuilderFactory`/`SAXParserFactory.newInstance()` with no recognized XXE guard in the same method — a default-configured XML parser resolves external entities, so crafted XML can read local files, perform SSRF, or exhaust memory. `disallow-doctype-decl` REJECTS THE DOCUMENT, NOT JUST THE ENTITY: with it set the parser raises a fatal `SAXParseException` on ANY input that carries a `<!DOCTYPE ...>`, benign ones included — XHTML, a DTD-validated industry format, an RSS feed that declares its own character entities, older build and config files — so an ingest path that has been accepting those starts rejecting one hundred percent of them on the first document after deploy. It at least fails loudly, at parse time, rather than quietly. Look at what this parser is actually fed before you pick between the two settings below; if nothing legitimate carries a DOCTYPE, the first one is both the strongest and the right one. Set `disallow-doctype-decl` to `true`; `FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING` alone does NOT disable external entity resolution and is not sufficient on its own. If DOCTYPEs are genuinely required, set both `external-general-entities` and `external-parameter-entities` to `false` instead. Each recognized guard pattern silences this finding independently (any one alone is enough to veto it).

A `new ObjectInputStream` construction and a `readObject(` call CO-OCCUR in this Java method — TWO INDEPENDENT patterns (`new\s+ObjectInputStream` and `\breadObject\s*\(`), not one dotted `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` chain — that dotted shape is never matched as such, and nothing links the call's receiver to the constructed stream, so a `readObject(` on an unrelated object satisfies the second pattern just as well — the regex is receiverless, so even the DECLARATION of a custom `private void readObject(ObjectInputStream in)` serialization hook matches it. No order is required either, and the reported line is the `readObject(` one, which is the trigger. When they ARE connected, Java's native deserialization invokes arbitrary code paths (gadget chains), so deserializing an attacker-controlled byte stream can lead to remote code execution. Kept at `warning` because this local analysis can't prove the deserialized payload is attacker-reachable — treat it as CRITICAL wherever the input actually comes from a request body/query/header/upload. Use JSON/Protobuf instead, or validate the stream with an allow-list `ObjectInputFilter`.

This line uses a template-engine syntax that emits UNescaped HTML: EJS `<%- %>`, Handlebars `{{{ }}}` triple-stache, or Mustache `{{& }}` — if any interpolated value is user-influenced, this is reflected/stored server-side XSS. Use the escaped output form instead (EJS `<%= %>`, Handlebars/Mustache `{{ }}`), or route the value through a vetted sanitizer when intentional raw HTML is actually required. Sibling boundary: `browser/unsafe-html-sink` catches the client-side DOM-sink half of this class (`innerHTML` assignment in browser code); this rule catches the server-side template-engine half that produces the HTML in the first place — complementary, not overlapping. Scoped to template file extensions only (`.ejs`/`.hbs`/`.handlebars`/`.mustache`/`.njk`/`.nunjucks`), since these tokens only mean "unescaped output" inside a template file. EJS's `<%- include('partial') %>` is excluded, and the exclusion is REQUIRED-SYNTAX rather than a taste call: EJS returns a partial's rendered markup as a string, so the escaped form `<%= include(...) %>` prints that markup as visible text — the unescaped form is the only one that composes templates at all, which is why EJS's own documentation writes it that way. The excluded shape is narrow on purpose, and the narrowing is ENFORCED by the pattern rather than merely intended: the argument must be a CLOSED string literal followed immediately by `,` or `)`, so `<%- include(userPath) %>` still fires and so does the concatenated `<%- include('partials/' + p) %>` — an earlier spelling of this exclusion only proved the argument STARTED with a quote, which silenced that second shape while this sentence claimed otherwise. A backtick literal counts only when it carries no `$`, so an interpolated `` <%- include(`views/${name}`) %> `` is a dynamic path and reports like the other two. What the partial itself emits is judged when this rule reads the partial's own file. Residual limitation, stated because the veto is coarser than the shape it names: an `exclude_pattern` is evaluated against the whole LINE, so a second raw-output tag sharing a line with an excluded include — `<%- include('head') %><%- bio %>` — is silenced along with it. Every template in the measured corpus put one tag per line, so nothing observed hits this, and 'not observed here' is not 'cannot happen'. Measured 2026-08-19 over 9 upstream trees: 16 of this rule's 17 findings were exactly `<%- include('...') -%>`, and the one that was not — a bare `<%- message %>` on a login page — is a genuine finding and still reports. (Pug's buffered `!= expr` form is deliberately NOT covered: it is lexically indistinguishable from Pug/Nunjucks's loose-inequality operator `!=`, so flagging it would false-fire on every `a != b` conditional — a never-guess omission, not an oversight.) Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-template-unescaped-output-ok` — but note `//` is not a comment in EJS/Handlebars/Mustache/Nunjucks, so an inline marker there renders as literal page output, and inline suppression isn't clean there — prefer the config-level disable (hint below).

A `res.send`/`res.write`/`res.end` call co-occurs with request input (`req.query`/`req.params`/`req.body`/`req.headers`) AND an HTML-shaped marker (a literal opening tag like `<div>`/`<html>`, or a `Content-Type: text/html` header) in the same function, with no sanitizer call anywhere in it — this is a co-occurrence heuristic, not a proof that the request value actually reaches the HTML output (same honesty as `db/multi-write-no-tx`'s documented approximation): it flags the shape, not a traced data flow. Escape/sanitize request-derived values before splicing them into HTML, set an explicit `application/json` content type for pure API responses, or use a template engine with auto-escaping instead of building markup by hand. Sibling boundary: `security/taint-flow` also does source+sink co-occurrence for `.ts`/`.tsx`, but its sink list does not include `res.send`/`res.write`/`res.end` — this rule covers exactly the class taint-flow misses. The reach gap widened on 2026-08-21 and the old spelling of this sentence no longer named all of it: taint-flow stops at `.ts`/`.tsx` deliberately (its own row says so), while this rule reads every extension the TypeScript frontend claims -- so `.js`, `.cjs`, `.mjs` as before, and now `.jsx`, `.mts` and `.cts` as well. A React tree is the case that matters there: its handlers are `.jsx`, and before the widening neither rule opened them.

A string literal that opens or closes an HTML tag (`"
"`, `""`, ...) is concatenated with a non-literal (`+ someVar` / `someVar +`) in a file that also mentions a `res`/`response`/content-type-`text/html` server-response context — building HTML by concatenating a variable into tag markup is an injection sink if that variable is user-influenced. Kept `warning` and deployed-surface-excluded because this is shape-only and FP-prone (logging strings, test fixtures, non-response string building all read the same way to a regex) — the `require_file` gate on a response/content-type mention is there specifically to bias this toward real server-response context rather than firing on every HTML-shaped concatenation in the repo. Use a template engine with auto-escaping, or a sanitizer, instead of hand-assembling markup. Sibling boundary: `html-response-from-request` needs the request-input+HTML-marker co-occurrence inside one function; this rule needs neither — it fires on the concatenation shape alone, so treat the two as complementary.

A filesystem call (`fs`/`fsp.*`, `readFile`/`writeFile`), request input (`req.params`/`req.query`/`req.body`), and a `path.join(...)` call all appear in the same function — this is a co-occurrence heuristic, not proof the request-derived value actually flows into the joined path, but when it does: an unvalidated `..` segment lets an attacker escape the intended directory (path traversal). Reject `..` segments, or verify the resolved path stays under the base directory.

rules._note: Rule id intentionally keeps its `java-` prefix: dropping it to `path-traversal` would collide with this pack's existing JS `path-traversal` rule (the Java `new File(...)` + `request.getParameter(...)` shape is distinct from the JS fs+path.join shape). The prefix earns its keep as a disambiguator.
rules.message: `new File(...)` is constructed in a method that also reads `request.getParameter(...)` — a CO-OCCURRENCE heuristic, not proof the parameter reaches the path: the two patterns may match unrelated statements in the same method, and nothing here checks order or dataflow (a `new File(...)` on a constant path in a method that reads an unrelated parameter fires just the same). It is deliberately weaker evidence than its TypeScript sibling `path-traversal`, which requires a third co-occurring `path.join(...)`. When they ARE connected, an unvalidated parameter flowing into the path lets an attacker escape the intended directory and read/write files outside it. Reject `..` segments, or resolve and compare against the base directory before use.

An outbound HTTP call (`fetch`/`axios`/`got`) is made in a function that also reads `req.query`/`req.params`/`req.body` — if that value becomes part of the URL, the server can be made to request attacker-chosen hosts (SSRF), reaching internal services or a metadata endpoint. The `if` is load-bearing: this is a CO-OCCURRENCE heuristic, not dataflow — the request read and the outbound call are matched independently inside one function body, so nothing here establishes that the read value reaches the URL, and a handler that reads a query parameter for something else while calling a hard-coded endpoint fires identically. Validating or allow-listing the target does NOT clear the finding either, since the veto would have to see a dataflow this matcher never had; suppress a vetted case with the inline marker instead. `warning` rather than `critical` for exactly that gap, the standing its sibling `security/path-traversal` takes. Validate the target against an allow-list of hosts.

`redirect(...)` is called in a function that also reads `req.query`/`req.params`/`req.body` — if the request-derived value is the redirect target and is unchecked, an attacker can send victims to an arbitrary external site (open redirect), a common phishing/OAuth-token-theft vector. Stated as a condition because this is a CO-OCCURRENCE heuristic, not dataflow: the two halves are matched independently within one function body, so the request read that put this function in scope MAY HAVE NOTHING TO DO WITH the redirect's target. What the target's own TEXT can settle is settled — a target that OPENS with a string or template literal whose first fragment PINS THE AUTHORITY DOES NOT FIRE AT ALL: a fragment starting `/` followed by anything other than a second `/` or a `\` is a same-origin path reference, and a fragment that already carries `?` or `#` HAS TERMINATED THE AUTHORITY, so nothing appended or interpolated after either one can move the origin. Everything else still fires whatever it holds — a bare identifier, a call, a template opening with an interpolation. Validate the target against an allow-list of known internal origins and let that validator produce the redirect's WHOLE value (`res.redirect(getSafeRedirectUrl(target) ?? "/home")`) — a call whose name carries a safety word (`safe`/`sanitize`/`allowlist`) AND a target word (`Url`/`Uri`/`Redirect`/`Link`) CLEARS this finding when it OPENS the argument and nothing that could move the origin follows it: the value may continue only into `??`/`||` fallbacks that are themselves calls or quoted literals, and the call may sit at the START of a template literal whose remaining text begins with `?` or `#` (the same authority rule as above). Read on the anchor line or on the continuation lines the call's own parentheses hold open. What the veto does NOT reach, and is therefore worth checking by hand before dismissing a finding: a validator applied on a PRECEDING statement or decided by a wrapper, one written below a comment inside the argument list, one whose value does not finish closing within 8 lines of the `redirect(` (the window is capped there, and the veto has to read the value's terminator), one CONCATENATED or interpolated beside a raw value in EITHER direction instead of producing the whole value (`getSafeRedirectUrl(base) + req.query.q` and `` `${getSafeRedirectUrl(base)}${req.query.next}` `` both still fire — a suffix that does not start with `?` or `#` can complete a hostname), and a line carrying two `redirect(` calls (which declines the veto outright rather than guessing which call it belongs to). The authority gate has a limit of the same kind: it reads only a literal SPELLED INSIDE the call, so a leading fragment held in a name one line up (`const base = "/section/"; redirect(base + input)`) still fires — resolving a name to its value is the same dataflow this layer does not do. Deliberately NOT treated as validation: a schema `.parse()` of the query — the measured shape prefixes a base URL onto RELATIVE targets and passes an ABSOLUTE `http(s)://` one through unchanged, so it reads as a guard while being none. One FALSE VETO this vocabulary cannot spell its way out of: `sanitizeUrl` (`@braintree/sanitize-url`) carries both halves of the name while doing a different job — it strips `javascript:`/`data:`/`vbscript:` protocols for XSS and passes an absolute `https://evil.com` through unchanged — so `res.redirect(sanitizeUrl(req.query.next))` is cleared here and should not be; judge the helper's body, not its name. The FALLBACK arm has the same shape of cost: a `??`/`||` fallback is admitted because it is a CALL, not because its value is safe, so `getSafeRedirectUrl(base) ?? String(req.query.next)` and `?? decodeURIComponent(req.query.next)` are cleared here and should not be -- and TypeScript pushes exactly those, since `req.query.x` is `string | string[] | ParsedQs` rather than `string`. A template fallback interpolating a BARE identifier is trusted the same way, and that identifier may hold a request value assigned one line earlier. Measured across both corpora: 36 of the 37 mitigated sites use this arm and NONE of them puts a request read in a fallback, so the arm stays and its cost is stated here rather than removed. `redirect` is matched lexically, so a local helper of that name counts too. `warning` rather than `critical` for that gap.

`sendFile`/`download` is called with a `req.params`/`req.query`/`req.body`-derived path — the sibling `path-traversal` rule catches `fs`/`path.join` reads built from request input in the same shape, but does not cover Express's file-serving APIs (`res.sendFile`/`res.download`) directly, so this rule fills that gap. An unvalidated `..` segment lets an attacker read arbitrary files off disk via path traversal. Reject `..` segments, or resolve the path and confirm it stays under the intended base directory, before passing it in. v1 is kept honest rather than clever: a same-line `path.basename(...)` call vetoes the finding by simple textual co-presence, not by proving it actually wraps the request-derived argument — a real sanitizer elsewhere in the function is not detected.

A digest the PARSER witnessed being constructed with a broken algorithm (MD5 or SHA-1) sits on a line that also names a credential (`password`/`passwd`/`pwd`) — those digests are too cheap to resist offline brute force at billions of guesses/sec on commodity GPUs. The credential-word half stays LEXICAL and stays a CO-OCCURRENCE: it proves the two appear on one line, not that this digest hashes that password — which is why this rule is `warning` and not `critical`, and why a line that REJECTS a weak algorithm while naming a credential reads the same to it. CHANGING THE ALGORITHM DOES NOT CHANGE WHAT THE OLD ONE ALREADY PRODUCED: every value already stored was produced by the broken algorithm and is readable only by it, so swapping the construction in place leaves those values unverifiable, and the break arrives at READ time, on live traffic, rather than at deploy. Plan the cutover before the edit — write with the new algorithm from the first deploy, keep the old one on a read-only path, record which of the two produced each stored value, and retire the old path once nothing it produced is left. Use bcrypt with a cost factor of at least 10, or argon2id/scrypt at OWASP-recommended memory/parallelism parameters — and because a password digest cannot be recomputed (the plaintexts are gone), that read-only path is the LOGIN path: verify a legacy row against MD5/SHA-1 at its next successful login and re-hash it with the new algorithm right there, then expire or force a reset on whatever never logs in again. Do NOT bulk-upgrade by re-hashing the stored digests: `bcrypt(md5(pw))` verifies fine and pins those accounts to MD5's input space permanently, so the accounts you meant to protect are the ones you froze there. WHAT COUNTS AS A HASH moved from a text regex to the parser's projected call-site channel on 2026-08-03, and the reach moved in three directions worth naming rather than discovering. It is NARROWER and more honest: the old arms matched the bare word `md5`/`sha1` anywhere on a line, so a variable, a parameter, an error message or a project's own helper named `md5` satisfied them exactly as well as a real digest construction — none of those fires now, and neither does an algorithm named only inside a string literal or a comment, because a mention is not a construction. It is WIDER by language: one rule covers TypeScript/JavaScript (`crypto.createHash`), Python (`hashlib`), Java (`MessageDigest.getInstance`), C# (`MD5.Create`/`HashAlgorithm.Create`), Go (`crypto/md5` and its siblings) and Rust (the `md5`/`sha1`/`sha2` crates), each with that platform's own spellings. And it is narrower in a way that costs recall, disclosed rather than discovered: a digest whose ALGORITHM the source does not spell at the site (`createHash(algoVar)`, `hashlib.new(name)`, `MessageDigest.getInstance(algo)`) carries no algorithm at all — never-guess — so this rule says nothing there, and the same holds for a file this engine cannot parse, for a hashing package no producer claims, and for a construction whose credential word sits on a different line. Silence here is absence of evidence, never a clean bill.

bcrypt invoked with a SINGLE-DIGIT cost factor passed AFTER the value being hashed (`bcrypt.hash(pw, 8)`, `bcrypt.hashSync(pw, 4)`) — each increment doubles the work, so a single-digit cost is orders of magnitude below the current recommendation and falls to offline brute force on commodity GPUs. Use a cost factor of at least 10; the unit is bcrypt-specific and is NOT a scrypt/argon2 parameter. This arm shipped inside `security/weak-password-hash` until the 2026-08-03 call-site migration and was split out rather than carried along, because it is a different claim about a different thing: its sibling now judges WHICH DIGEST the parser witnessed being constructed, while a bcrypt cost factor is a numeric ARGUMENT to an adaptive hash that is itself the recommended answer — there is no digest construction to witness, so the structural channel has nothing to say here and the check stays lexical. Being lexical it is a one-line shape match, with the limits that implies: a cost passed through a constant (`bcrypt.hash(pw, COST)`) or configured elsewhere is invisible to it, and it reads a literal digit only. Both argument POSITIONS are covered — the cost after the value being hashed (`bcrypt.hash(pw, 8)`), and the salt-first family where it comes first (`bcrypt.genSalt(4, cb)`, `bcrypt.genSaltSync(4)`, and the nested `bcrypt.hashSync(pw, bcrypt.genSaltSync(4))` that bcryptjs's README documents).

`Math.random()` is used on the same line as a token/otp/nonce/session-id/secret-shaped identifier — it's a predictable PRNG, not cryptographically secure, so a value generated this way can be guessed or brute-forced. THE SWAP CHANGES THE VALUE, NOT ONLY THE GENERATOR, AND IT DOES NOT REACH THE VALUES ALREADY ISSUED: `randomBytes(n).toString(hex)` yields 2n characters over a 16-symbol alphabet and `randomUUID()` yields a fixed 36-character form with dashes, so neither matches the length or the character set the `Math.random()` expression produced — a fixed-width column, a checksum, a display format or a six-digit OTP contract fails on the first write rather than at the call. Check where the value is stored and compared before you change how it is made, and size the replacement to the column rather than to the example. `crypto.randomBytes` is Node — in code that also builds for a browser, an edge runtime or a Worker there is no `node:crypto` to import, and the replacement there is `crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(n))` from the Web Crypto API. Every value minted before this edit stays predictable: changing the generator does not invalidate them, so the ones still accepted have to be expired or reissued separately. Use `crypto.randomBytes(n).toString('hex')` or `crypto.randomUUID()`.

`new Random()` is used on the same line as a token/session/otp/nonce-shaped identifier — `java.util.Random` is a predictable PRNG, not cryptographically secure, so a value generated this way can be predicted or brute-forced. Use `java.security.SecureRandom` instead.

A digest the PARSER witnessed being constructed with a broken algorithm (MD5, MD2 or SHA-1) — these have practical collision attacks (forgeable signatures/certificates), so they are the wrong tool for tokens, cache keys, signatures and content addressing alike. AN HMAC IS NOT A BARE DIGEST, AND THIS RULE FIRES ON BOTH. `crypto.createHmac("sha1", key)` builds an HMAC, and SHA-1's collision attacks do NOT break HMAC-SHA1: HMAC's security rests on the compression function behaving as a PRF, not on collision resistance, and no practical forgery against HMAC-SHA1 is known. So the collision sentence above is a claim about a BARE digest standing in for a signature; on a `createHmac` line the true reading is narrower — HMAC-SHA1 is DEPRECATED for new protocols and a new one should be HMAC-SHA-256 — and treating the two as the same fact overstates what is known about the HMAC. It fires on the HMAC anyway, because the deprecation is real, but the rule does not separate the two and the message will not pretend it does. Nor is the coverage even-handed across languages, which is worth naming rather than discovering: `createHmac` sits inside the TypeScript producer's `hash-call` family, while Go's `crypto/hmac`, C#'s `HMACSHA1`, Rust's `hmac` and Python's `hmac` are each deliberately OUTSIDE theirs (all four on the same stated ground — an HMAC's strength is its inner hash's, which the site does not spell). An HMAC-SHA1 therefore fires here in TypeScript/JavaScript and is invisible in every other language this rule covers. AND THE ALGORITHM MAY NOT BE YOURS TO PICK — the case that turns the remedy below from unhelpful into harmful, and the one this rule cannot see because it reads the construction and not the protocol. Where the digest verifies a signature a COUNTERPARTY produced — an inbound webhook (`x-vercel-signature` and friends), an OAuth 1.0a request, a legacy partner callback — the SENDER fixes the algorithm and the receiving side has no freedom at all. "Use SHA-256" there hardens nothing: it rejects the genuine requests instead, all of them, and usually before any comparison runs, because a SHA-256 hex digest is 64 characters where SHA-1's is 40 and a length check fails first. Change what you SIGN or what you SPECIFY; where you only VERIFY what somebody else signed, the fix is a protocol change agreed with that counterparty, and until they ship it the site is a tracking item rather than an edit. THOSE THREE ARE EXAMPLES, NOT THE WHOLE LIST — and all three are on the VERIFY side. A short exemption list that ends by telling you to proceed everywhere else turns its own INCOMPLETENESS into a push: the reader walks it, honestly matches nothing, and makes the dangerous edit BECAUSE they were diligent. Two questions decide a site the list does not name. Does this position CHOOSE the algorithm, or RECEIVE one somebody else already chose? And is anything this algorithm already produced still alive somewhere that has to keep accepting it? The second catches what the list above cannot — the ISSUING side, where your own program mints a value here and your own program checks it in another file: a two-site protocol with no counterparty in it, which breaks from the inside. CHANGING THE ALGORITHM DOES NOT CHANGE WHAT THE OLD ONE ALREADY PRODUCED: every value already stored was produced by the broken algorithm and is readable only by it, so swapping the construction in place leaves those values unverifiable, and the break arrives at READ time, on live traffic, rather than at deploy. Plan the cutover before the edit — write with the new algorithm from the first deploy, keep the old one on a read-only path, record which of the two produced each stored value, and retire the old path once nothing it produced is left. THAT LANDING ASSUMES A STORED VALUE, AND THE ISSUING SIDE OFTEN HAS NONE: a secret DERIVED per call — a digest of a user identifier and a server key, behind a one-time code — is recomputed, not persisted, so there is no row to migrate and nothing to record. What outlives the edit is what is already IN FLIGHT, codes already mailed and links already sent, so the read-only path is a CLOCK rather than a migration: it lasts one validity window, retires itself, and until it does the old derivation has to keep answering. And that derivation is normally spelled out at BOTH the issuing site and the checking site, which this rule reports as two findings in two files — change the one you were shown and the two sides derive different secrets, reaching the user as an invalid-code error rather than as anything traceable. Change every site that derives the same value in ONE commit. Use SHA-256 or stronger; for passwords specifically use bcrypt/PBKDF2/argon2id (that credential-line special case is `security/weak-password-hash`, and the two rules CO-FIRE on one line by design — they say different things about it). WHAT COUNTS AS A HASH moved from a Java-only text regex to the parser's projected call-site channel on 2026-08-09, the same move `weak-password-hash` made first, with the same three reach directions worth naming rather than discovering. NARROWER and more honest: a variable, a parameter or an error message named `md5`, or an algorithm spelled only in a comment or an unrelated string, no longer fires — a mention is not a construction. (The commons-codec `DigestUtils.md5*` helper family also no longer fires: it encodes the algorithm in a method NAME rather than a construction argument this channel witnesses — zero uses measured in this repo's corpus and cases the day of the move.) WIDER by language: TypeScript/JavaScript (`crypto.createHash`), Python (`hashlib`), Java (`MessageDigest.getInstance`), C# (`MD5.Create`), Go (`crypto/md5` and siblings) and Rust (the `md5`/`sha1` crates), each in that platform's own spelling. And narrower in a way that costs recall, disclosed rather than discovered: a construction whose algorithm the source does not spell at the site (`createHash(algoVar)`, `hashlib.new(name)`) carries no algorithm at all — never-guess — so this rule says nothing there, and silence is absence of evidence, never a clean bill. And narrower by FILE SCOPE, the fourth direction, disclosed the same way: the old line-scan also admitted `.jsp`/`.jspx`/`.tag` files, and the call-site channel projects no sites from JSP scriptlets — so JSP hash constructions are no longer judged at all, and their silence too is absence of evidence (`security/weak-cipher` still reads JSP for the cipher arms). And narrower by DECLARATION, the fifth direction: a Python construction whose SAME LINE also says `usedforsecurity=False` is skipped. That keyword is CPython 3.9+'s own statement that a digest is not a security primitive (bandit honours it as B324), so it is evidence the source WROTE, not an inference about intent — the only kind admissible for a suppression. It is honoured as a DECLARATION rather than as proof: a digest that is security-adjacent despite carrying it is skipped too, because a scanner that overrules an explicit author declaration on a guess about intent is doing the thing this engine refuses everywhere else. RESIDUAL, measured rather than implied, and it has THREE parts. The check reads the call's WINDOW — its own line plus the continuation lines ITS OWN parentheses hold open — so a construction a formatter split across lines is covered since 2026-08-21; on getredash/redash @ ca79fe98 that is 3 of the tree's 5 `usedforsecurity` uses, which fired until then. FIRST, a declaration OUTSIDE those parentheses is out of reach by construction: a keyword set on a preceding statement, or a wrapper that decides for it. SECOND, the window is capped at 8 continuation lines, so a declaration further inside a very long argument list still fires. THIRD, and the one worth knowing about because it costs a WAIVER rather than a finding: when two calls to the same function share one line, this check cannot tell which occurrence the site is, so it declines to open a window at all and reads the line alone — `md5(a).hexdigest() + md5(\n  b, usedforsecurity=False\n)` reports BOTH digests, the declared one included. Declining is deliberate: the first version of this window counted the LINE's parentheses rather than the call's, and a `(` inside a string, inside a trailing comment, or belonging to an enclosing call each let a DIFFERENT call's declaration waive a real finding. Absence of the keyword is absence of a declaration, never a statement that one was refused. The cipher half of the old rule (DES/RC4/ECB) lives in `security/weak-cipher` now.

A `Cipher.getInstance(...)` transformation names a broken cipher or mode — DES/RC4/RC2 are brute-forceable or biased, and ECB encrypts equal plaintext blocks to equal ciphertext blocks, leaking message structure. CHANGING THE ALGORITHM DOES NOT CHANGE WHAT THE OLD ONE ALREADY PRODUCED: every value already stored was produced by the broken algorithm and is readable only by it, so swapping the construction in place leaves those values unverifiable, and the break arrives at READ time, on live traffic, rather than at deploy. Plan the cutover before the edit — write with the new algorithm from the first deploy, keep the old one on a read-only path, record which of the two produced each stored value, and retire the old path once nothing it produced is left. Use AES-GCM (or another AEAD mode) — and unlike a password digest this data IS recoverable, so that read-only path is a DECRYPT path and the cutover is a re-encryption: decrypt each record with the old transformation as it is read (or in a batch pass), write it back under the new one, and delete the legacy path only when no record still carries the old tag. Where the ciphertext crosses a boundary you do not own — a peer service, a stored export, a client that decrypts it — that side has to accept the new form BEFORE you start emitting it, or it stops being able to read you the moment you deploy. Re-encrypting also does not un-leak what DES or ECB already exposed to anyone holding a copy: treat that plaintext as disclosed and rotate whatever it protected. SCOPE, stated rather than discovered: this rule reads Java/JSP sources only — `Cipher.getInstance` is the JCA factory and the only cipher-construction spelling this engine judges today; cipher constructions in other languages are unmeasured, not endorsed. Until 2026-08-09 these arms lived inside `security/weak-crypto` (which now carries the hash half, six languages wide, on the parser's call-site channel), so a `// zzop-weak-crypto-ok` marker left on a cipher line predates the split and no longer suppresses it — re-vet the line under this rule's own marker.

A secret/token/signature/hmac/api-key-shaped identifier is compared with `===`/`!==` — equality operators short-circuit on the first differing byte, so the comparison time itself can leak a timing signal about the value to an attacker positioned to measure it. TWO QUESTIONS DECIDE WHAT TO DO HERE, AND `crypto.timingSafeEqual` THROWS RATHER THAN ANSWERING `false` IF YOU SKIP THEM. (1) ARE BOTH SIDES SECRET VALUES SOMEONE IS TRYING TO GUESS? This rule reads the identifier's NAME, so a state/enum/config comparison whose name merely contains a secret-shaped word matches the spelling with no secret on either side, and browser code has no `crypto.timingSafeEqual` to reach for in the first place — those are examples rather than a list, and the question that sorts your case is whether a caller who could submit millions of guesses would learn anything from how long this line takes. If not, this line is already correct. (2) CAN THE TWO SIDES DIFFER IN BYTE LENGTH? `crypto.timingSafeEqual` throws `RangeError [ERR_CRYPTO_TIMING_SAFE_EQUAL_LENGTH]` on unequal byte lengths and `TypeError [ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE]` when handed plain strings, so passing it a request-supplied value and a stored secret — the exact shape this rule flags — replaces a failed auth check with a 500 on every wrong guess, and `String.length` is not the guard: it counts UTF-16 code units, so one accented character makes a five-character string six bytes and two equal-`.length` strings still throw. WHERE BOTH SIDES ARE SECRETS, hash each side to a fixed width and compare the digests — `timingSafeEqual(createHash('sha256').update(a).digest(), createHash('sha256').update(b).digest())` is 32 bytes on both sides for any input, so it answers `false` where the direct call would have thrown. This rule judges only `===`/`!==`, so that rewrite clears the finding on its own.

TLS certificate/hostname verification is disabled (a trust-all `X509TrustManager`, `ALLOW_ALL_HOSTNAME_VERIFIER`, or a `setHostnameVerifier` lambda always returning `true`) — accepts any certificate for any host, so the app can't detect a man-in-the-middle. RESTORING VERIFICATION IS NOT A NO-OP WHERE THE TRUST-ALL WAS LOAD-BEARING, AND IT FAILS AT RUNTIME RATHER THAN AT BUILD: this is usually written the way it is because the peer presents something the default trust store will not accept — a certificate signed by an internal CA, a self-signed staging host, an appliance reached by IP so the hostname never matches the SAN, a TLS-inspecting corporate proxy — and once the default verifier is back, every call to that peer throws `SSLHandshakeException`/`CertificateException` instead of returning, starting with the first request after deploy. Find out what the peer actually presents before you make the edit, because the answer picks the fix: if the chain is genuinely private, TRUST it rather than trusting everything — load that CA into a `KeyStore`, build a `TrustManagerFactory`/`SSLContext` over it, and hand that to the client, which keeps the call working and still detects a man in the middle. If the certificate is instead wrong, expired, or issued for another name, that is a real defect on the server and this edit is what makes it visible. Use the default (or a properly validating custom) trust manager/verifier.

`jwt.sign(...)` is called where `expiresIn` never appears in the same function — a token with no expiry is valid forever, so a leak (logs, XSS, a compromised client) can be replayed indefinitely. ADDING AN EXPIRY DOES NOT REACH THE TOKENS THIS FINDING IS ABOUT. `exp` is a claim inside the signed payload, fixed at the instant each token was minted, so every unbounded token already in circulation keeps verifying exactly as it did — a verifier that passes no `maxAge` has nothing to check it against. The edit below therefore closes this finding and leaves the whole at-risk population untouched; retiring that backlog is a SECOND step, and it is the expensive one, because the two things that invalidate an already-issued token — rotating the signing secret, or making the verifier REQUIRE `exp` — take effect on all of them at once, ending every live session and 401-ing any sibling service that verifies with the same secret (`security/jwt-sign-literal-secret` owns the sequencing for the rotation half). Plan both halves before doing either: pass `{ expiresIn: '...' }` (or set `exp` in the payload) so newly issued tokens expire, then choose when to retire the outstanding ones and tell whoever owns those sessions beforehand rather than afterwards. TWO THINGS TO CHECK AT THIS CALL SITE FIRST: whether it is a shared signing helper, where one default lifetime lands on every caller that never asked for it; and whether anything is expected to still hold a token past the lifetime you are about to pick — a device with no refresh flow, a machine-to-machine integration, a link with the token embedded in it. Those are two instances of one question: who has to present this token after the deadline you are setting, and what renews it for them?

`algorithm(s): 'none'` appears in a JWT-related file — `alg: none` turns signature verification off entirely, so a caller can mint an arbitrary token that validates with any payload it wants. There is no legitimate production use of this algorithm. EVERY TOKEN ALREADY IN CIRCULATION WAS MINTED UNDER THE OLD LIST, AND THIS EDIT IS WHAT STOPS ACCEPTING THEM: `alg` is a header parameter inside the token's own signed-over bytes, so narrowing the verifier re-issues nothing — at the instant of deploy every unsigned token already held by a browser, a mobile client, a cron job or a sibling service is rejected, and that arrives as a 401 rather than as a prompt to sign in again. Unlike the other cutovers in this pack there is no overlapping window to plan, because an `alg: none` token cannot be honoured for even one more request: the sessions END, and what has to be sequenced instead is the CLIENTS — check that a 401 drives them to re-authenticate rather than into a retry loop, and cut over any sibling service that still MINTS `none` in the same deploy or its calls start failing too. Pin the verifier to the algorithm you actually issue rather than to the first one named below: a fleet part-way through an `HS256`-to-`RS256` change that pins only one half stops verifying its own live tokens for the same reason. Remove `none` from the allowed/signing algorithm list and use a real algorithm (`HS256`/`RS256`/...), pinning `algorithms` explicitly on the verifying side too so a future token can't downgrade itself. Suppress a vetted case (e.g. a local test harness that intentionally exercises the none-alg attack) with `// zzop-jwt-none-algorithm-ok`.

`ignoreExpiration: true` or `verify: false` appears in a file that imports a JWT library (`jsonwebtoken`/`jose`/a `jwt` specifier) — either option turns off a check `jwt.verify` exists to perform: `ignoreExpiration: true` accepts an expired token, `verify: false` accepts one with no signature check at all (an outright auth bypass). The require-file gate on a JWT-library import is load-bearing here: bare `verify: false` also appears in plenty of unrelated configs (bundlers, linters, ...), and without the gate this rule would fire on those too. Remove the option (or set it to the safe default) so `jwt.verify` performs its normal checks.

CORS origin set to `*` (a wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header, `origin: '*'`, or a Rust framework's allow-any idiom) — lets any website make cross-origin requests to this endpoint, defeating same-origin protection. A wildcard is legitimate for a purely public, credential-less API (no cookies/auth headers involved) — suppress that case with `// zzop-cors-wildcard-ok` rather than "fixing" it. Return a specific allow-listed origin instead, especially on endpoints that accept cookies or auth headers. The Rust arms match the dominant idioms by their own spelling rather than the wire header: tower-http's `.allow_origin(Any)` (any path-qualified spelling of `Any`), actix-web's `.allow_any_origin()`, and the typed constant `ACCESS_CONTROL_ALLOW_ORIGIN` paired with a `"*"` literal on the same line. Spellings beyond those — a wildcard reached through a variable, a config file, or a framework not named here — are NOT seen; for them only the literal header text arm applies.

`credentials: true` appears in a file that also configures `origin: '*'` — the pairing is FILE-level, not object-level: the two keys are matched anywhere in the same file, so they may belong to two unrelated config objects (a wildcard-origin public CORS block and a separate credentialed one) and still fire. Browsers actually REJECT (refuse to expose the response for) a wildcard `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` combined with credentials, so this exact configuration is broken/non-functional rather than exploitable as written. The real risk: to "fix" the breakage, code often reflects the request's `Origin` header back with `credentials: true` still set — that treats any origin as trusted and IS the actual vulnerability. Return a specific allow-listed origin (never `*`, never an echoed `Origin`) whenever `credentials: true` is set. Both matched keys are JS OBJECT-LITERAL shapes (`credentials: true`, `origin: '*'`), not wire-header values, so this rule deliberately scans JS/TS only — Rust/other-language CORS config is builder-call shaped and is not judged here (unlike the sibling `cors-wildcard`/`csp-weak-or-disabled`, whose header-value arms do scan `.rs`).

`credentials: true` co-occurs on one line with `origin: true` (cors()'s reflect-any-origin mode) or `origin: req.headers...` (manually echoing the request's Origin header) — either shape treats any origin as trusted while allowing cookies/credentials, which is the actual exploitable CORS misconfiguration (unlike a literal `'*'`, which browsers reject alongside credentials). Sibling boundary: `cors-wildcard`/`cors-credentials-wildcard` cover the literal `'*'` shape; this rule covers the REFLECTION shape those two miss. Return a specific allow-listed origin instead of reflecting the request's origin. Known limitation, not desired behavior: this is a single-line co-occurrence check, so a multi-line CORS options object (each key on its own line) is missed — see the pinned fixture documenting this gap.

Content-Security-Policy is explicitly turned off or weakened: Helmet's `contentSecurityPolicy: false`, a `Content-Security-Policy` header value containing `unsafe-inline`, or a `default-src` directive containing a wildcard `*` — CSP is the browser's last line of defense against XSS once a payload has already been injected, so disabling/weakening it removes a mitigation that has nothing to do with whether the injection itself is possible. TIGHTENING CSP IS ENFORCED BY THE BROWSER THE MOMENT IT SHIPS, AND IT BLOCKS BEFORE IT REPORTS: enabling Helmet's default policy, or dropping `unsafe-inline`, stops every inline `<script>`/`<style>`, every `on*=` attribute handler and every widget or analytics snippet that injects one — including third-party ones you do not control — and the affected page renders blank with console errors rather than failing a build or a test, so a green pipeline is not evidence the rollout is safe. THE ORDER THAT AVOIDS THAT: ship the intended policy on `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` FIRST, collect violations from real traffic long enough to cover the routes your tests never open, wire a per-response nonce (or hashes) into every inline block those reports name, and only then move the same policy onto the enforcing header. Keep a restrictive policy: enable Helmet's default CSP (or a hand-configured one) instead of `false`, drop `unsafe-inline` in favor of nonces/hashes, and scope `default-src`/`script-src` to specific allow-listed origins instead of `*`. The two header-value arms are wire-header shapes, so this rule also scans `.rs` (a Rust service setting the literal `Content-Security-Policy` header is judged exactly like a JS one); the `helmet-csp-false` arm is a JS-library option key and is silent in `.rs` by nature — arm-level silence in one language, not rule-level silence. Kept at `warning` because this is a mitigation-ABSENCE rule (defense-in-depth), not proof of an exploitable injection by itself.

A cookie is set (`res.cookie`/`setCookie`) without `httpOnly` in the same function — a session/auth cookie without it is readable by any script on the page, so an XSS bug becomes full session theft. HIDING IT FROM SCRIPTS IS WHAT THE FLAG DOES, SO ANY CLIENT CODE THAT READS THIS COOKIE BY NAME STOPS SEEING IT — AND STOPS SILENTLY: a helper that scans `document.cookie` returns `undefined` for a hidden cookie exactly as it does for an absent one, so nothing throws at the edit and the loss surfaces later as a logged-out user or a request missing a header. Search your client for this cookie's name before making the change. The cases that legitimately need a script-readable cookie are the ones where the BROWSER is a reader too — a double-submit CSRF token the client copies into a request header, a locale or theme value read during hydration — and those are examples rather than a list, so the question that sorts your case is whether anything other than the server ever reads this cookie back. IF THE SERVER IS THE ONLY READER, add `{ httpOnly: true }`. IF SOMETHING IN THE CLIENT READS IT, that value does not belong in the same cookie as the session: split it in two and keep `httpOnly` on the half that authenticates. `secure` and `sameSite` are separate decisions this finding does not make for you, and each has its own breakage — `secure: true` withholds the cookie from any plain-HTTP origin (a non-TLS local or internal host stops receiving it), and a lax/strict `sameSite` withholds it from cross-site requests (an embedded widget or a cross-origin POST that depended on it stops being authenticated). Suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-insecure-cookie-ok`. This rule judges only the two spellings whose framework default is httpOnly=FALSE; `cookies.set` is deliberately NOT one of them, because on SvelteKit that call defaults to httpOnly=TRUE and the absent option is the correct code.

A raw error object is sent directly to the client (`res.status(5xx).send/json(err)`, or Hono's `c.json(err)`) — errors often carry stack traces, file paths, or internal config that help an attacker map the system. Log server-side and send a generic message (e.g. `{ error: 'Internal server error' }`) instead.

A stack-trace call (`printStackTrace()`, `getStackTrace()`) and an HTTP-response token (`getWriter()`, `ResponseEntity`, `@ResponseBody`, `HttpServletResponse`) both appear in the same method — this is a co-occurrence heuristic, not proof the trace is written to the response (a `printStackTrace()` that goes to stderr in a method that merely mentions `HttpServletResponse` fires too). When the trace does reach the client, it exposes internal class names and file paths. Log server-side and return a generic error body instead. (A custom exception's `.getMessage()` — a curated message string, not a stack trace — is deliberately NOT flagged, to match this rule's stack-trace-exposure scope.)

A token/JWT-shaped value is written to `localStorage` — readable by any script on the page, so a single XSS bug anywhere on the origin can exfiltrate it with no further exploitation. Default fix: store it in an `httpOnly` cookie with `sameSite` set, plus CSRF-token protection. This isn't a full fix either — cookies reintroduce CSRF risk (mitigated by `sameSite`/CSRF tokens), and an active XSS bug can still ride an existing cookie session in-place — but it does stop direct token theft/exfiltration. Accepted alternative: an in-memory access token with a rotating refresh token, or a Backend-For-Frontend (BFF) pattern.

`req.body` (or a spread of it) appears in a function that ALSO performs a database write (`create`/`update`/`upsert`/`updateMany`) — if the request object is what reaches that write, an attacker can set any field the model accepts (role, isAdmin, price, ownerId, ...) that the handler never intended to expose. This is a CO-OCCURRENCE heuristic, not dataflow: the two halves are matched independently within one function body and nothing links them, so a `req.body` that goes somewhere else entirely and an unrelated write on another line produce exactly this finding — measured on `logger.info({ ...req.body })` followed by a `create` whose `data` is all constants, where the finding anchors on the LOGGER line. That is why it is `warning` and not `critical`, the same standing its siblings `security/taint-flow` and `security/path-traversal` take for the same reason. The reverse also holds: a write fed by a variable assigned from `req.body` in an earlier statement is the shape this rule is named for, and it is matched only because both tokens happen to sit in the same body, never because the assignment was followed. Whitelist the fields you accept, or use a validated DTO.
